transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Well, it's... I mean, I guess I'm here because things have just gotten really out of hand lately. It’s mostly about eating. I don't even know how to explain it properly without sounding completely insane, but... well, when I start eating—and this happens a lot, especially if I'm back in my dorm and stressed out about my classes or just alone with my thoughts—once I take that first bite, it's like I completely disappear. 

It's like my actual self just vanishes and something else entirely takes over my body. And the worst part is, I'm still in there somewhere, you know? Like, in the back of my head, I'm literally screaming at myself, telling myself to just stop, to put the food down, but my hands just keep moving. I just keep going and going, eating everything until I physically can't stand it anymore, until I feel so full it actually hurts. It's just so terrifying because no matter how hard I try to just be normal about a meal, that... that *thing* just hijacks me, and I have absolutely zero control over myself once it starts. I just can't stop.
Do you ever feel detached from yourself or like you're outside of your body even when you're not eating or about to eat?

No, not really. Honestly, no. Like, if I'm just walking to my morning lecture—my intro to bio class is all the way across campus, so I have a lot of time to just walk and think—or if I'm just sitting in the library trying to study, I feel totally normal. Well, maybe not *normal*, because I'm usually pretty stressed out about my grades and keeping my scholarship and everything, but I definitely feel like *me*. 

I'm completely in my body. I feel my feet on the ground, I hear the people talking around me, I'm entirely aware of every single thing I'm doing. It's actually kind of the opposite of being detached, because I'm almost hyper-aware of everything, you know? Like, I can feel every bit of that college pressure just sitting right there in my chest, heavy and real. 

So, no, I don't get that floaty, out-of-body feeling when I'm just going about my regular day. And I think... I think that's why the food thing is so incredibly messed up and scary to me. Because I go from being this completely grounded, maybe overly-stressed freshman who is just trying to pass his classes and be a regular guy, to suddenly being completely hijacked the second I'm alone with a box of cereal or whatever. It's strictly when the food is there. The rest of the time, I'm just me, stuck in my own head, but definitely still in my own body. It's just the eating that does it.
When you're eating during these episodes, do you feel like you can't stop eating or control what or how much you're eating, even if you want to?

Yeah, exactly. Like I was trying to explain when I first sat down, that is exactly what happens. It's a hundred percent that feeling of just... not being able to stop, no matter how desperately I want to. I mean, it's not like when you're hanging out with friends and you just eat too much pizza because it tastes good and you're not paying attention. It's nothing like that. It's this total, terrifying loss of the steering wheel. 

Like, just the other night—I think it was Tuesday—my roommate was out at a study group, so I was alone in the room. I opened this family-size bag of chips, just meaning to have a handful because I was staring at a blank screen for my bio lab report and I was feeling that heavy chest anxiety I mentioned. But then... it's like a switch flipped. The thing took over. I ate the whole bag in minutes. And I didn't even want to! Halfway through, my brain is literally screaming at me, going, "Dude, stop, you're going to feel sick, you don't even taste this anymore, you're just chewing." But my hands... my hands just kept reaching into the bag, over and over, like they were being operated by remote control. 

And it didn't stop there. When the chips were gone, I tore into a whole sleeve of cookies, and then some leftover takeout from the mini-fridge, and I just... I couldn't stop myself. I was sitting there on my bed, feeling so disgusted, wanting to just put the food down and walk away, but I couldn't. I just kept shoving it in until my stomach was stretched so tight it actually felt like it was going to tear open, until I physically couldn't fit another bite without being in agony. So, yeah, to answer your question, even if I want to stop with every fiber of my being, I absolutely can't. The brakes are completely cut once I start.
After these episodes of eating where you feel like you can't stop, do you ever try to compensate for it by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising excessively?

Yeah... yeah, I do. I mean, I have to, right? Because after I eat all that—after the whole bag of chips and the cookies and whatever else I can find—this overwhelming panic just sets in. It's like this cold sweat, and my heart starts hammering in my ears, and all I can think about is all that food just sitting inside me. Just sitting there, heavy and gross, turning into fat, turning into weight that I can't afford to gain. 

So, immediately after it happens, the guilt is just... it's suffocating. I feel so disgusting and so full that I can barely breathe, and the only way to make that panic stop, the only way to undo what that *thing* just made me do, is to get rid of it. So I usually end up sneaking off to one of the bathrooms in the dorm. Or, if I'm studying late and it happens, I know which floors in the library are usually empty, so I'll go to a bathroom there. I'll lock myself in a stall, turn on the sink or flush the toilet so no one can hear me, and I just... I make myself throw up. 

It's awful, it really is. My throat burns, my eyes water, and my knuckles get all scraped up against my teeth, but in that moment, I just feel so terrified of the food staying inside me that I don't care. I just have to get it out. I have to empty myself out so I can feel clean again, or at least so I don't feel like I'm going to explode. It's this whole exhausting cycle—the anxiety, the eating, the panic, and then the bathroom. And I hate it, I really hate it, but once the binge happens, throwing up just feels like the only option I have left to fix it.

Do you have episodes of eating large amounts of food in a short period of time even when you’re not physically hungry, and do these episodes happen on their own without you trying to make yourself vomit or do anything else afterward?

Well, for the first part of what you're asking, about eating a lot when I'm not actually physically hungry... yeah, absolutely. It really has nothing to do with hunger at all. I mean, half the time my stomach is already completely full before I even start. 

Like, there have been nights after studying—especially lately, because the reading load for my history seminar is just ridiculous and I'm stressing out, up until like 2 AM trying to take notes—where I go from the dining hall, where I just had a full meal, straight back to my room. And even though I'm not hungry in the slightest, I just start eating. I'll eat burgers I brought back, bowls of cereal, giant spoonfuls of peanut butter straight out of the jar, random snacks I have stashed in my desk, literally whatever I can get my hands on. It's way, way more than a normal dinner, and I just keep going and going until the trash is completely full of wrappers and empty boxes, and I feel physically sick. I'll look at that overflowing little dorm trash can and just think, 'How did I even fit all that in?' It's just massive amounts of food. 

But to answer the second part of your question, about whether it ever happens without me doing anything afterward... no. Never. It never, ever happens on its own without me trying to fix it. Like I was explaining just a minute ago, I could never just let all those burgers and cereal and peanut butter sit inside me. The guilt and that heavy, terrifying panic I mentioned, it's just too intense. I would lose my mind if I just had to sit there and digest it all. So I never just have an episode like that and then go to bed or go back to studying. I always, always have to go to the bathroom to get rid of it. I just couldn't survive the anxiety if I didn't.
